title: Bridging retrieval and KV-cache: summer reading notes
content:
Top-level goal:
Quick distillation of multiple recent reads on how retrieval strategies and KV/prefix caching interact with cost/latency in serving LLMs. Brain dump for follow-up experiments and a short list of practical heuristics we could test on the Redwood runtime (dedicated + hosted).

Motivation/context:
- We want to reduce per-token compute (and latency) while preserving effective context. Retrieval allows giving the model extra grounded context without inflating autoregressive sequence length, but it also adds latency/cost from the retrieval step and subsequent attention on concatenated input.
- KV/prefix caches keep model state across turns or earlier context; combining them with retrieval could enable much longer effective context at low marginal cost — if we avoid cache thrash and irrelevant cache growth.

Papers/blogs skimmed (quick takeaways):
1) "Sparse Retrieval + Cache Composition" (internal notes + arXiv paper)
   - Core idea: retrieve small, high-signal chunks and store them as compressed KV entries keyed by semantic id; reuse across similar queries.
   - Pros: avoids re-attending to entire long context; KV lookup cost << full forward pass.
   - Cons: requires robust similarity hashing and eviction heuristics; mismatch between retrieval embedding space and model's attention relevance can cause stale hits.
   - Experiment idea: maintain per-customer semantic-id fingerprints and measure hit precision/recall vs. direct-attend baseline.

2) "Latent Prefixing and Soft Cache" (conference talk notes)
   - Not full retrieval: compute a learned compact prefix vector to summarize a long doc; prefix injected into early layers as conditioning.
   - Interop with KV: could treat prefixes as a special kind of KV entry (smaller, less granular).
   - Risk: learned prefixes can drift when data distribution shifts (privacy/regulatory concern when prefixes summarize PII).

3) "Economics of Batching vs. Retrieval" (engineering blog)
   - Key trade-off: batching reduces amortized kernel overhead but increases tail latency; retrieval reduces token length but adds separate request overhead.
   - Operational note: on Dedicated clusters we can co-locate retrieval services on the same nodes to reduce network hops — measure 95p latency before claiming a cost win.

4) "KV Eviction Strategies: TTL vs. Relevance Score" (lab notebook)
   - TTL (time-based) is simple but brittle; relevance-based eviction using recency+semantic-similarity crumb performs better in synthetic workloads.
   - Combine: soft TTL (decay factor) + min-relevance threshold.

Mini-summaries: what I think matters most for Redwood experiments
- Hit quality beats hit quantity: small, high-precision retrieval that maps to meaningful KV chunks is better than just caching everything.
- Compression matters: storing compressed KVs (4-8x) reduces instance memory pressure and reduces eviction churn. We need to try different compression quant/ops tradeoffs (int8, q4_0, QAT for prefix vectors).
- Routing and co-location: retrieval lookup, embedding, and KV access should ideally be implementable as colocated microservices to keep latency low. For hosted API, network cost is nontrivial.

Concrete experiment slate (priority order):
1) Baseline measurement: measure end-to-end latency and cost for (a) long prompt-attend baseline, (b) retrieval + concat + attend, (c) retrieval + KV-lookup + partial attend. Use two workloads: chat-like (many short turns) and doc-summarization (single long doc).
   - Metrics: 50/95/99 latency, token compute (GPU ms/token), cost estimate per 1k requests, output quality (ROUGE/QA accuracy on a small eval set).

2) KV compression sweep: test raw KVs, 8-bit quant, and vector-compressed (PCA/kmeans) prefixes for hit quality vs. memory footprint.

3) Eviction policy ablation: TTL-only, recency+relevance, soft-decay with min-threshold. Track hit precision and downstream QoE.

4) Routing policy prototype: add a policy in the runtime to prefer cached-KV hits before falling back to retrieval; measure false positives (stale hits) and latency savings.

Operational notes / quick wins:
- Add simple instrumentation to the cache layer: store metadata (last_access_ts, semantic_score, origin_retrieval_id) for post-hoc analysis. Low-cost logs for the first month will pay back.
- When measuring quality, use human-checks on ~200 examples for hallucination risk — automated metrics miss subtle grounding failures.
- Small hack: prefer retrieval embeddings computed by the same encoder used at serving time to avoid embedding-space mismatch.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much does quantizing stored KVs hurt generation when used as full-context vs. prompt prefix? (We need a microbenchmark.)
- Can we maintain privacy guarantees if cached prefixes summarize user data? Need to talk to security/compliance before rolling to private deployments.
- Is there a sweet spot for chunk size (128 vs 512 tokens) that balances retrieval precision and cache footprint?

Short action items (who/when):
- Victor: build the baseline measurement harness (7 days) and wire in token-level compute logging (GH draft: redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments PR).
- Mira: quick eval set construction (50 chat threads + 30 doc-summary tasks) — due in 4 days.
- Evan: prototype compressed KV storage (PCA-based) and run memory footprint comparison on a c5.xlarge dev node (10 days).

Notes-to-self: keep these notes messy. When we have preliminary numbers, move a cleaned-up one-pager to shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/ so SRE/team can see results. Also, ask product-hosted-api about acceptable tail-latency SLAs for retrieval pre-checks.

References & links (quick):
- arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12731 (retrieval+cache survey)
- Internal GH issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/issues/42
- Slack convo: #kv-cache-sync (pinned messages)

End of scratchpad.
